ClarityCheck is a facial recognition tool that makes it hard to imagine any legitimate use for it. Recently, there have been reports that it publicly exposed millions of face photos on the internet, constituting a major privacy breach.

The vast majority of victims are likely completely unaware, never knowing that their photos were uploaded to the site, and never authorising such practices……

The service allows anyone to upload photos of others in order to reverse-search social media and other platforms to identify them. Although ClarityCheck requires users to agree that they have the right to upload, cybersecurity research expert Jeremiah Fowler expressed extreme doubt about this to Wired.

The site's blog posts include entries such as "Find someone on a dating site via email" and "How to find someone on Hinge (even without matching)."

Farrell, in an interview with ExpressVPN, pointed out that the over 9 million image files uploaded to ClarityCheck were publicly exposed on a cloud server for several months, and stated that these files were mainly facial images, including some cropped and resized duplicates.

I recently discovered a publicly exposed database with no password protection and no encryption. The database contained approximately 9,042,977 image files, totalling 450.2GB. The leaked data consisted mainly of facial images stored in folders named "faces" and "profiles." In the limited sample of images I reviewed as part of my investigation, I observed that they included facial images of adults, teenagers and children [……] Many of the uploaded images I saw appear to have originated from third-party sources, such as private social platform accounts, social media accounts, dating app accounts, screenshots, or physical photos uploaded by third-party users.

He traced the database back to ClarityCheck, which confirmed ownership of the relevant data and stated that the database had been re-locked.

9to5Mac's view

One of the risks Fowler identified is that scammers could use these photos and the associated identity information to create fake social media posts impersonating others to deceive their friends and family. A common scam involves impersonating a family member in an emergency and demanding an immediate wire transfer. Obtaining facial photos would undoubtedly facilitate such fraudulent activities.
